title: Converting an advantage: take, exchange or keep the pressure
outcomes: Sorts the candidate moves in a winning position into taking material, exchanging and a quiet move
Checks that a tempting capture or exchange does not hand back the advantage
Recognises when a clean capture or an exchange really is the best conversion

steps.text:
A big lead still has to be turned into a win. There are three ways: **take material**, **exchange pieces**, or play a **quiet move** that keeps the opponent tied down. Each has a cost: a capture can open lines, an exchange can ease his position, a quiet move gives him time.
Before you grab, ask which move leaves him the fewest useful replies.

steps.caption: White is far ahead. Qxc4 wins a pawn at once; the quiet Be3 is also possible.

line.say: Be3: the bishop steps back and every piece stays on.
Black puts a knight on e5.

claims.statement: At depth 16 White is at least 350 centipawns ahead.
The engine's best moves are Be3 and Bf4, equal at depth 16.
Qxc4 is at least 400 centipawns worse than the best move.

steps.text: No kind of conversion is always right. **Rule of thumb:** with a crushing lead, take the quickest forced win or a clean capture; with a large but not yet decisive lead, keep the pressure and avoid trades that give the opponent air. Winning does not mean you may stop calculating: check the capture you want and the exchange you want before you play them.

steps.title: Three ways to convert
steps.prompt: In each position White or Black is far ahead. Predict first whether taking, exchanging or a quiet move is best. The third position is a different case.
Think of a game where you were winning and it slipped. Which of the three ways did you use, and which would you choose now?
